title: Lease-Up Turns a Building Into a Business
summary: A rental building is worth what its income is worth, and on the day it opens it has almost none. Lease-up is the period in which a finished building becomes a stabilised business, and it is decided by four things: the pace of leasing, the real rent after concessions, the quality of operations and the contracts that run the property. This lesson sets out how to think about each.
body:
On completion day a rental building is an expensive object with almost no income. Lease-up is the work of turning it into a business with a stable rent roll, and the value you will be paid for, by a lender or a buyer, is the value of that business, not of the object.

Recall

Q. In Week 124, what were the four families of pre-sale rules?

A. Disclosure and cooling-off, deposit protection, honest marketing and buyer verification, with a further line where a home sold with a guaranteed return may become a security.

Q. What is a limitation period?

A. The time the law allows to start a claim, after which it is usually barred; for hidden construction defects it may run from discovery rather than completion.

Q. What is a lien waiver?

A. A document in which a contractor or supplier gives up lien rights for amounts already paid, collected with each payment so the owner does not pay twice.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in a rental or hotel project, your loan is usually repaid by a take-out loan or a sale, and both are sized on stabilised net operating income. Until the building is leased and running at its expected occupancy, you carry interest, operating costs and marketing with too little income to cover them. A slow or careless lease-up can cost more than a construction overrun, and it is more within your control. This lesson is the frame for the week. LEX covers landlord-tenant law and management agreements on Day 4.

The lease-up curve

In plain English: tenants arrive at a pace, not all at once, and income follows them.

The professional framing is the lease-up curve: occupancy plotted against time from opening, rising from near zero to stabilised occupancy, the level the building is expected to hold in normal conditions after allowing for turnover and vacancy. Absorption, which you met in Week 28, sets the slope. Stabilisation is a defined point, usually a sustained occupancy level for a set period, and lenders define it in their own terms, which are commercial practice.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 120-unit building, stabilised occupancy of 95 percent, which is 114 units. If the market absorbs 12 net leases a month, stabilisation takes about 9.5 months. At 8 a month it takes about 14 months. If each occupied unit earns 2,000 dollars a month and the building's fixed operating costs run 90,000 dollars a month from day one, the slower curve leaves you carrying several extra months of costs and interest with partial income. That difference is often hundreds of thousands of dollars, and it lands exactly when your contingency is spent.

Face rent and effective rent

In plain English: the rent on the lease is not the rent you earn if you gave something away to win the tenant.

The professional framing separates face rent, the stated rent in the lease, from effective rent, the rent after concessions such as free months, move-in credits or paid moving costs, spread over the lease term. Concessions are the main price lever in lease-up, because they let you hold face rent, which appraisers and buyers often read from the rent roll, while competing on price.

A second worked example. Face rent 2,000 dollars a month on a 12-month lease, with one month free. Total rent received is 11 months times 2,000, or 22,000 dollars, so effective rent is 22,000 divided by 12, about 1,833 dollars a month, 8.3 percent below face. If a lender or buyer values the building on face rent without adjusting, they overvalue it. If you report face rent without the concession, you are the one who has overstated it. Always report both.

Say that out loud now.

Operations are the product

A new tenant does not experience your structure or your capital stack. They experience the leasing office, the move-in, the first maintenance call and the noise from the unit above. Operations, delivered by a property manager or, for a hotel, an operator, decide renewals, reviews and the reputation that drives the next lease. A property management agreement typically sets the manager's fee, often a percentage of collected revenue, its authority to sign leases and spend money, its reporting duties and how either side may end it. A hotel management agreement does the same for an operator, usually with a base fee on revenue, an incentive fee on profit, a long term and an owner's right to terminate on poor performance under defined tests. These are commercial terms, negotiated deal by deal.

The rent roll is the record that ties it together: one line per unit, with tenant, lease dates, face rent, concessions, deposit and status. A buyer or lender will test it lease by lease against signed leases and the bank account. Build it that way from the first lease.

Renewals are the second lease-up

Most first-year leases expire at about the same time, because the building filled in a few months. That creates a second test, twelve or so months after opening, that new owners often forget: a wave of renewals. If concessions were used to win the first tenants, each renewal is also the moment you try to remove them, and the tenant compares your renewal offer with the free month the building next door is still advertising.

A short illustration, hypothetical. Sixty leases expire within three months. If 55 percent renew, you need to re-let 27 units in the same quarter you are trying to stabilise, while also paying turnover costs for cleaning, repairs and marketing, perhaps 1,500 dollars a unit, about 40,000 dollars. If 70 percent renew, you re-let 18. The difference is nine fewer turnovers and weeks of vacancy avoided. Two controls help: stagger lease terms during lease-up, offering some tenants 9-month or 15-month leases so expiries spread out, and start renewal conversations early. The renewal rate is the first honest measure of whether your operations are working.

How the best do it

Strong operators plan lease-up before construction ends. They open a leasing office and a model unit months ahead, pre-lease from a waiting list, staff the maintenance team before the first move-in and track a weekly leasing funnel: enquiries, tours, applications, approvals and move-ins. A small developer can copy this by hiring the property manager while the building is still under construction and agreeing the funnel report and its targets in the management agreement.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the date a building is placed in service, and how lease-up costs are treated, can affect depreciation and deductions; ask a tax adviser before opening. Liability: operations carry premises liability and tenant claims, so insurance and the manager's duties must match. Banking: the take-out loan is sized on stabilised income, so the lease-up curve is a loan risk. Governance: the manager's spending and leasing authority must be written limits. Estate: a stabilised building with clean records is easier to hold or pass on. Exit: a buyer prices the rent roll, so its accuracy is value.

Professional sign-off required: a lawyer admitted where the building is, for the lease form and the management agreement.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is buying occupancy with concessions you do not report, so that the rent roll looks stronger than the income. The control is a rent roll that shows face rent, concessions and effective rent for every lease, reconciled monthly to bank receipts.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hires the property manager on opening day. By then the leasing season, the waiting list and the staffing decisions are already behind you. Hire during construction.

Callback

In Week 14, Sage taught vacancy, lease-up and stabilised NOI as lines on a pro forma. This week those lines become people, contracts and weekly numbers. The assumption you typed in a spreadsheet three years earlier is now tested one tenant at a time.

Recap

Lease-up turns a finished building into a business. Its pace sets your carry, effective rent after concessions sets your real income, operations set renewals, and the rent roll is the evidence a lender or buyer will test. Plan it during construction.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: Stuyvesant Town, and a rent roll the law would not allow.
checklist: I know the lender's definition of stabilisation and the occupancy it requires.
My lease-up curve is based on measured absorption, with a slow case beside the base case.
I know my monthly carrying cost from opening day: operating costs, interest and marketing.
Every lease in the rent roll shows face rent, concessions and effective rent.
The rent roll is reconciled to bank receipts every month.
The property manager or operator is appointed during construction, with a funnel report in the agreement.
The manager's leasing and spending authority are written limits.
A local lawyer has approved the lease form and the management agreement.
head: Field checklist
speak: On completion day a rental building has almost no income, and lease-up turns it into a business. Four things decide it. The lease-up curve: occupancy rises at the market's absorption pace to stabilised occupancy, and in my hypothetical 120-unit building, 12 leases a month stabilises in about 9.5 months and 8 a month takes 14, which costs months of carry. Effective rent: one free month on a 12-month lease at 2,000 dollars face rent means about 1,833 dollars effective, 8.3 percent less, and I report both. Operations: the property manager or hotel operator delivers the product the tenant actually experiences, under an agreement with fees, authority limits, reporting and termination rights. And the rent roll: one line per unit, tested lease by lease against signed leases and the bank. I hire the manager during construction, not on opening day.
terms: Stabilisation — the point at which a building reaches and holds its expected normal occupancy and income, as defined by the lender or the business plan.
Effective rent — the rent actually earned after concessions such as free months, spread over the lease term.
Rent roll — the schedule of every unit or lease showing tenant, dates, rent, concessions, deposits and status.

hostile.q: As the take-out lender, your rent roll shows 2,000 dollars average rent. Why should I size my loan on that?
hostile.a: You should not size it on face rent alone, and I would not ask you to. The rent roll shows face rent, concessions and effective rent for every lease. Average effective rent on the leases signed in the last 90 days is about 1,833 dollars, because we offered one month free during lease-up. Concessions are tapering as occupancy rises, and I will give you the funnel report and bank reconciliation so you can see the trend rather than take my word for it.

title: Stuyvesant Town: A Rent Roll the Law Would Not Allow
summary: In late 2006 a very large Manhattan apartment complex was bought on a plan to lift rents by moving regulated apartments to market rents. A 2009 court ruling held that many of those deregulations were not allowed, and in early 2010 the owners handed the property to their lenders. Taken through the seven forensic steps, with Cole assisting on the legal side, the case shows why a rent roll must be tested against the law that governs each lease.
body:
The buyers of Stuyvesant Town did not misjudge the market so much as the law. Their plan depended on rents rising faster than the legal status of the apartments allowed, and when a court said so, the income the debt was sized on did not exist.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between face rent and effective rent?

A. Face rent is the rent stated in the lease; effective rent is the rent actually earned after concessions such as free months, spread over the lease term.

Q. What is Rule 124?

A. Never let a buyer's deposit fund anything but the building it was paid for; hold deposits in protected trust or escrow, sell only what the funded plan can finish and never use pre-sale cash for land or another project.

Q. What is debt yield?

A. Net operating income divided by the loan amount, a measure lenders use because it does not depend on the interest rate or the cap rate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Ford, with Cole assisting on the legal side. Lease-up is usually discussed as a question of demand: will tenants come, and at what rent? This case is about a different question that every rental owner faces: is the rent you plan to charge one the law allows you to charge? I will keep to the public outline of events. I quote no prices, and I do not draw any conclusion about New York law beyond what the outline states. Verify the legal detail against the primary source before you rely on it.

1. Timeline

Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village is a very large complex of apartment buildings on the east side of Manhattan, built after the Second World War by an insurance company that owned it for decades. Many of its apartments were rent stabilised, a form of rent regulation under New York law that limits increases and gives tenants renewal rights. In late 2006 the owner sold the complex to a venture led by a large real estate company and an investment manager, in a deal widely reported as one of the largest residential transactions in American history, financed with a large amount of debt. The business plan relied on moving regulated apartments to market rents as they became vacant or qualified for deregulation. In 2009, New York's highest court ruled, in a case brought by tenants, that apartments in buildings receiving a particular property tax benefit could not be deregulated in the way many had been while the benefit was received. In January 2010 the owners announced they would turn the property over to their creditors.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions carried the failure. Paying a price that only worked if a large share of regulated apartments moved to market rent within a few years. Financing that price with high leverage, so that the debt service depended on the future rent roll rather than the current one. And treating the deregulation path as a business assumption rather than a legal question with a real chance of being decided against the owner.

3. Assumptions

The plan assumed the rate at which apartments would turn over and move to market rent, that market rents would keep rising and that the legal route to deregulation was secure. The first two were market assumptions that a weaker economy from 2008 made worse. The third was the one that broke the deal, because it was not a forecast at all. It was a reading of a statute, and the reading was disputed.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

In a competitive bidding process for a trophy asset, the bidder with the most optimistic rent growth wins. Lenders in 2006 competed for large loans in a market full of credit. Advisers and brokers were paid on closing. Nobody in the chain was rewarded for discounting the price to reflect the chance that a court would read the law differently. The tenants, by contrast, had every incentive to test that reading, and they did.

5. Warning signs ignored

Cole's view. The legal question was visible. The property was known to receive tax benefits, and tenant advocates had raised the deregulation issue publicly. A buyer's legal due diligence could have treated the deregulation path as a contested question, assigned it a probability and priced it. The plan's income, meanwhile, was well above what the existing regulated rent roll produced, so the debt was sized on rents that did not yet exist. When a loan is sized on income that depends on a legal outcome, the legal outcome is credit risk.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the closing itself. Once the price was paid and the debt drawn, there was no way to reduce the leverage if the rent plan failed, and the court case would take years to decide. The ruling in 2009 did not create the problem. It removed the possibility that the plan would work.

7. Root cause

The root cause was underwriting a rent roll that had not been tested, lease by lease, against the law that governed each lease, and then borrowing against the untested version. A small-scale sketch with hypothetical round numbers shows the mechanism. A buyer pays for a 100-unit building on a plan to raise 40 regulated units from 1,200 to 2,000 dollars a month. That lifts annual rent by 384,000 dollars. At a 5 percent cap rate, that is about 7,700,000 dollars of value. If a court rules the increases unlawful, the 384,000 dollars of income disappears, the value disappears with it, and the loan sized on that value is now larger than the building can support.

The question every rental buyer should ask

You will never buy an asset that size, but you will buy or refinance rental buildings whose rent rolls contain the same kind of question. Rent regulation, tenant protection rules, tax incentive conditions, affordability covenants in a development agreement and existing lease renewal rights can all limit what a unit may legally earn. Each one can sit quietly in a document you did not draft. The habit that would have changed this outcome is simple: before you price an increase in rent, ask your lawyer in writing whether that increase is legally available for each unit, what conditions apply and whether any of them are being disputed by tenants or authorities. Then price the answer as a probability rather than a certainty.

The prevention rule

Rule 125: never underwrite or borrow against a rent you have not tested, lease by lease, against the law that governs that lease. Treat any rent that depends on a change in a tenant's legal status as a legal risk to be priced, not as a business assumption to be forecast.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a rent roll built from the spreadsheet rather than from the leases and the law. The control is a lease audit before purchase or take-out: every lease read, its regulatory status confirmed by local counsel and the rent schedule rebuilt from what each lease legally permits.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes that because rents are below market they can be raised to market. Whether they can depends on the lease, the law and sometimes on benefits the building has received. Ask before you pay for the difference.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering the rent and return implied by a price. Applied here, it would have shown the market immediately what rent the price required. The step that was missing was to ask a lawyer whether that rent was legally available, and to price the answer.

Recap

A late-2006 purchase of a large Manhattan complex depended on deregulating apartments faster than the law allowed. A 2009 court ruling held many deregulations were not permitted, and in January 2010 the owners handed the property to creditors. Rule 125: test every rent against the law that governs its lease before you underwrite or borrow against it.

Next: Sage on The Money: what lease-up costs, and how it moves value and the take-out loan.
checklist: Every lease in a rent roll I underwrite has been read, not summarised.
Local counsel has confirmed the regulatory status of every unit before purchase or take-out.
I know whether the building has received any benefit that limits rent increases.
Any rent that depends on a change in legal status is priced as a legal risk with a probability.
My loan is sized on current, lawful income, with upside treated as equity's risk.
My business plan shows the value at today's lawful rent roll beside the target.
I record pending tenant claims and regulatory disputes as risks in the deal file.
head: Field checklist
speak: In late 2006 a very large Manhattan apartment complex, many of whose apartments were rent stabilised, was sold in one of the largest residential deals ever reported, financed with heavy debt. The plan relied on moving regulated apartments to market rents. In 2009 New York's highest court ruled that apartments in buildings receiving a particular tax benefit could not be deregulated as many had been, and in January 2010 the owners handed the property to their creditors. The mistake was less about the market than the law. The debt was sized on rents that depended on a disputed reading of a statute. In a hypothetical 100-unit building, raising 40 regulated units by 800 dollars a month adds about 7.7 million dollars of value at a 5 percent cap rate, and a ruling can remove it in a day. Rule 125: test every rent against the law that governs its lease before underwriting or borrowing against it.
terms: Rent stabilisation — a form of rent regulation that limits increases and gives tenants renewal rights, under rules that vary by place.
Lease audit — reading every lease in a rent roll and confirming its terms, status and lawful rent, rather than relying on a summary.
Deregulation — moving an apartment out of rent regulation so it can be let at market rent, permitted only in the circumstances the law allows.

hostile.q: As your equity partner, our business plan assumes 30 percent of units move to market rent in three years. Why are you discounting it?
hostile.a: Because that increase depends on each unit's legal status, and I have not yet got a written opinion from local counsel that the path is available. I have shown the deal at today's lawful rent roll and at the plan, with the difference treated as upside for equity, not as income the loan is sized on. If counsel confirms the path, the upside is still there. If not, we have not borrowed against rent we cannot charge. That is Rule 125.

rule: Rule 125: Never underwrite or borrow against a rent you have not tested, lease by lease, against the law that governs that lease; treat any rent that depends on a change in a tenant's legal status as a legal risk to be priced, not a business assumption to be forecast.

title: What Lease-Up Costs, and How Concessions Reach the Take-Out Loan
summary: During lease-up you carry the full cost of a finished building on part of its income, and the gap has to be funded. At the end of lease-up, the take-out loan and the building's value are both set by stabilised net operating income, so every concession that becomes permanent reaches the loan and the value. This lesson prices both with hypothetical round numbers.
body:
Lease-up costs money twice: first as an operating deficit while the building fills, and then, if concessions become the market's normal rent, as a permanently lower income that shrinks both the take-out loan and the value. Price both before you open.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 125?

A. Never underwrite or borrow against a rent you have not tested, lease by lease, against the law that governs that lease; treat any rent that depends on a change in legal status as a legal risk to be priced.

Q. What is an interest reserve?

A. A budget line inside the construction loan that pays the loan's own interest during construction and, often, lease-up, so that interest does not have to be paid from income the project does not yet have.

Q. What is the exit cap rate?

A. The capitalisation rate assumed for the sale or valuation of the finished, stabilised asset, used to convert its net operating income into value.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a rental project's construction loan is normally repaid by a permanent or take-out loan once the building is stabilised. If the stabilised income is lower than planned, the take-out is smaller, and the difference between the construction loan and the take-out has to come from your equity. That is a cash call at the end of a project, when you may have least cash and most guarantees. Lease-up is where that number is decided.

The operating deficit

In plain English: from opening day you pay for the whole building, but you collect rent only from the units that are let.

The professional framing is the operating deficit: operating costs plus debt service minus collected revenue, month by month, until income covers costs. Lenders often require it to be funded from an interest reserve or an operating deficit reserve in the budget, or guaranteed by the sponsor. The sizing is commercial practice.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 120-unit building with a 22,000,000-dollar construction loan at 7 percent interest only, which is about 128,300 dollars of interest a month. Operating costs are 90,000 dollars a month from opening. Face rent is 2,200 dollars, with one month free on a 12-month lease, so effective rent is about 2,017 dollars. Lease-up runs about 10 months, so average occupancy across lease-up is about half the building, roughly 57 units. Average collected revenue is about 57 times 2,017, or about 115,000 dollars a month. Costs are 128,300 plus 90,000, about 218,300 dollars a month. The deficit is about 103,300 dollars a month, or about 1,030,000 dollars across lease-up. If your budget reserve for it is 600,000 dollars, you are 430,000 dollars short, and every extra month of slow leasing adds about 100,000 dollars more.

Concessions reach the take-out loan

A second worked example, same building, at stabilisation. Gross potential rent at 2,200 dollars face is 120 units times 2,200 times 12, which is 3,168,000 dollars. Less 5 percent vacancy, effective gross income is about 3,009,600 dollars. Less operating costs of 1,080,000 dollars a year, net operating income is about 1,929,600 dollars.

The take-out lender sizes on a debt yield of 8 percent, a commercial term for this hypothetical. The maximum loan is NOI divided by 0.08, about 24,120,000 dollars. That repays the 22,000,000-dollar construction loan with room to spare.

Now suppose the market will not let you remove the free month, and effective rent stays at about 2,017 dollars. Gross income at effective rent is about 2,904,000 dollars, less 5 percent vacancy about 2,758,800 dollars, less operating costs, NOI about 1,678,800 dollars. The maximum take-out at an 8 percent debt yield is about 20,985,000 dollars. You are now about 1,015,000 dollars short of repaying the construction loan, and that is an equity call.

Say that out loud now.

Value follows the same line. At a 5.5 percent cap rate, NOI of 1,929,600 dollars is worth about 35,080,000 dollars, and NOI of 1,678,800 dollars is worth about 30,520,000 dollars. A concession that looked like a marketing tactic is a 4,560,000-dollar difference in value. That is why the face rent on a rent roll is never enough: a lender or buyer will price the concessions in the most recent leases, and so should you.

Hotels: the same idea with a daily rent

For a hotel, lease-up is called ramp-up, and the income measures are average daily rate, occupancy and revenue per available room, known as RevPAR, from Week 29. A new hotel usually takes a period of years to reach stabilised RevPAR, and during ramp-up the operator's base fee, charged on revenue, is paid even while the hotel loses money. The money question is the same: how big is the deficit, who funds it, and what stabilised profit will the take-out lender size on. Many hotel lenders size on a trailing period of actual results, so a slow ramp-up delays the take-out as well as reducing it.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, the end of lease-up is the moment a development becomes an income asset. Two lines change. Contingent liabilities should shrink, as completion and cost guarantees fall away, though many take-out loans still carry recourse carve-outs; confirm what survives. And your equity at cost becomes equity at value, which is tempting to spend. Value is not cash. Record it, but keep your liquidity floor in cash and keep any equity call at take-out funded before you count the value as yours. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Time and energy, a monthly thread

Lease-up is a slow, weekly grind of small numbers: enquiries, tours, applications, move-ins. On a rotating shift schedule, it is easy to review it in irregular bursts, after a run of nights, when judgment is at its worst. Research on shift work and sleep, which Kema covered in Week 4, is consistent that fatigue impairs decisions; check with your doctor about your own sleep.

A practical habit is to fix one review slot each week on a rest day, after a full sleep, and to keep the funnel report short enough to read in ten minutes. Make no pricing or concession decision in the hour after a night shift. The weekly slot keeps the trend visible, and the rule keeps a tired mind from cutting rents to make a bad week feel better.

Who funds the gap

Before opening, write down who funds each part of the lease-up cost. The interest reserve inside the construction loan usually covers interest until it runs out. An operating deficit reserve, if the budget has one, covers operating shortfalls. After both, the sponsor funds, often under a carry or completion guarantee. Know the month each reserve is expected to run dry on the slow case, and tell the lender before it happens, not after. A lender told three months ahead can extend a reserve or agree a plan. A lender told on the day sees a default.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating concessions as temporary when the market has made them permanent. The control is to size the take-out and the value on effective rent from the most recent leases, not on face rent, and to fund the gap before it is called.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sizes the operating deficit reserve on the planned lease-up pace with no slow case. Size it on a slow case, and know the monthly cost of each extra month.

Callback

In Week 45, Nadia and Priya taught exit financing and the maturity gap between a construction loan and its take-out. Today shows where that gap is made: in the effective rent of the last fifty leases signed before stabilisation.

Recap

Lease-up costs an operating deficit, here about 1,030,000 dollars over 10 months, and, if concessions stick, a lower stabilised NOI that cut the take-out by about 3,135,000 dollars and value by about 4,560,000 dollars. Size both on effective rent and a slow case.

Next: LEX on The Rules: landlord-tenant law and management agreements, with Two Systems.
checklist: I have calculated the monthly operating deficit from opening day: operating costs plus debt service minus collected revenue.
My operating deficit reserve is sized on a slow lease-up case.
I know the cost of each extra month of lease-up.
I size the take-out loan on effective rent from the most recent leases, not face rent.
I know the take-out lender's sizing test, debt yield or coverage, and the loan it implies.
I have a funded plan for any gap between the construction loan and the take-out.
I review the leasing funnel at one fixed weekly slot, rested, and make no pricing decision after a night shift.
head: Field checklist
speak: Lease-up costs money twice. First, the operating deficit: from opening day I pay operating costs and interest on the whole building but collect rent only on the units let. In my hypothetical 120-unit building with a 22 million dollar loan, that deficit is about 103,000 dollars a month, about 1.03 million over a 10-month lease-up. Second, concessions. At 2,200 dollars face rent, stabilised NOI is about 1.93 million dollars, which supports a take-out of about 24.1 million at an 8 percent debt yield. If the free month never goes away, effective rent stays about 2,017 dollars, NOI falls to about 1.68 million, the take-out falls to about 21 million and I owe the construction lender about a million dollars of equity. Value falls by about 4.56 million at a 5.5 percent cap rate. So I size the reserve on a slow case and the take-out on effective rent.
terms: Operating deficit — the monthly shortfall when operating costs and debt service exceed collected revenue during lease-up.
Take-out loan — the permanent loan that repays the construction loan once a building is stabilised.
Ramp-up — the period in which a new hotel builds toward its stabilised occupancy, rate and RevPAR.

hostile.q: As your take-out lender, I will size on the trailing three months of effective rent, not your pro forma. Are you ready for that?
hostile.a: Yes, and I have already modelled it. On effective rent from the last 90 days of leases, NOI is about 1,680,000 dollars, which supports about 21,000,000 dollars at your 8 percent debt yield, against a construction balance of 22,000,000. I have reserved the difference as equity, and concessions on new leases are falling as occupancy rises. If you can wait one more quarter, the trailing figure improves; if not, the gap is funded.

title: The Rules of Letting: Tenants, Managers and Operators
summary: A rental building runs on three sets of rules: landlord-tenant law, which protects the people living there; the property management agreement, which governs the agent who runs it; and, for a hotel, the management agreement with the operator. This lesson sets out each as a concept and then compares how Canada and Guyana approach residential tenancy.
body:
Once tenants move in, your building is governed by rules you did not write and cannot contract out of, and by agreements with the people who run it that you did write and must live with for years. Know which is which before the first lease is signed.

Recall

Q. In yesterday's lesson, why did a permanent concession cut the take-out loan?

A. Because the take-out is sized on stabilised net operating income, and a free month that never goes away lowers effective rent and therefore NOI; at an 8 percent debt yield the loan fell by about 3,135,000 dollars.

Q. What is an agent's fiduciary duty?

A. The duty of a person acting for another to act loyally in that person's interest, avoid undisclosed conflicts and account for money and property held for them.

Q. What is a non-disturbance agreement?

A. An agreement in which a lender promises that, if it enforces its security, it will respect an existing lease or management agreement as long as the tenant or operator is not in default.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, residential tenancy is among the most protective areas of law in many places, because it concerns people's homes. Many of its rules cannot be waived by contract, and a lease clause that tries to waive them may simply be unenforceable. Your management agreements, by contrast, are mostly matters of negotiation, and a poor one can tie you to an underperforming manager or operator for years. This lesson teaches concepts and how to think, not what any jurisdiction requires. Verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it, and use a local lawyer for the lease form and the agreements.

Landlord-tenant law: five recurring themes

In plain English: the law usually decides how much deposit you may take, how you must keep the home, when you may enter, how rent may change and how a tenancy may end.

The professional framing lists five themes that recur across many regimes. Deposits: limits on the amount, rules on where it is held and when and how it must be returned. Repair and habitability: a duty to keep the premises in a fit state and comply with health and safety standards, often regardless of what the lease says. Entry and privacy: notice before entering except in emergencies. Rent: in some places, limits on increases, notice periods or registration under rent regulation. Ending the tenancy: defined grounds and procedures, usually through a tribunal or court, with self-help eviction, such as changing locks, prohibited in many places. Anti-discrimination law also governs who you may refuse and how you advertise. Each theme varies widely by place [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example, hypothetical. Your lease form, borrowed from another city, asks for two months' rent as a security deposit and says the landlord may enter on 4 hours' notice. In your jurisdiction, suppose the law caps deposits at one month and requires 24 hours' notice. The extra deposit may have to be refunded, perhaps with a penalty, and the entry clause is unenforceable. Multiply by 120 leases and the defect becomes a class of claims. The control is a lease form drafted for the jurisdiction, by a local lawyer, before the first lease.

The property management agreement

A property manager is your agent. The agreement should set its authority, such as the rent range it may sign leases at and the spending limit for repairs without your approval; its fee, commonly a percentage of collected revenue plus leasing fees, which is commercial practice; its reporting, including a monthly rent roll, bank reconciliation, arrears report and leasing funnel; how it holds money, ideally in a trust or client account in your name; and how either side may end the agreement and hand over records. Agency law generally adds duties of loyalty and accounting, but write them in anyway.

Say that out loud now.

The hotel management agreement

A hotel management agreement is more powerful, and more dangerous to an owner, than a property management agreement. The operator usually runs the hotel under its brand and systems, employs or directs the staff and controls day-to-day operations. Owners negotiate for a few critical protections: approval of the annual budget and capital plan, a performance test that lets the owner terminate if the hotel falls below an agreed benchmark for a set period, limits on the operator's ability to charge for central services, clear rules for key money or operator contributions, and what happens on a sale. Long terms and limited termination rights are common, and all of it is commercial practice negotiated deal by deal.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The agreement lets you terminate if, for two consecutive years, the hotel's RevPAR falls below 90 percent of a defined competitive set and operating profit falls below 90 percent of budget, with the operator allowed a cure payment. In year 3 RevPAR is 85 percent of the competitive set, but operating profit is 92 percent of budget. The test is a two-part test, and one part passes, so you cannot terminate. Owners lose performance arguments on the wording far more often than on the facts. Read the test as a lawyer would, with real numbers in it, before you sign.

Money held for others

One practical theme runs through all three sets of rules: money that belongs to someone else. Tenants' security deposits, rent collected by a manager and hotel revenue collected by an operator are each held for another party, at least for a time. Many regimes require deposits to be held separately, and good agreements require collected rent and hotel revenue to go into accounts in the owner's name, with the manager or operator drawing on them only within approved budgets. When money for others and money for operations share one account, a dispute or an insolvency of the manager can freeze both. Keep them apart from the first day.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source. In Canada, residential tenancy is largely provincial: provinces have their own residential tenancy statutes, many with a specialised tribunal or board that hears disputes, and rules on deposits, notice and rent increases differ from province to province, with rent controls in some [unverified — confirm independently]. Guyana's system descends from English common law, and it has legislation dealing with rent restriction and the recovery of possession of some premises, historically under a Rent Restriction Act; its current scope, the premises it covers and the procedure for recovering possession should be confirmed with local counsel [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical lesson for an owner in either place is to start from the statute and the forum, not from a borrowed lease form.

Professional sign-off required: a lawyer admitted where the building is, for the residential lease form, the property management agreement and any hotel management agreement.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a lease form or management agreement copied from somewhere else. The control is drafting both for the jurisdiction, reviewing them against the five tenancy themes and the owner protections above, and having counsel sign off before the first lease.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a tenant who stops paying can be removed quickly. In many places recovery of possession takes a defined legal process and time. Budget for arrears and process, and never use self-help.

Callback

In Week 30, LEX taught encumbrances and condominium declarations as things that run with title. Leases and some management agreements behave the same way in practice: a lender, a buyer or an heir takes the building subject to them. A badly drafted agreement is an encumbrance you created.

Recap

Landlord-tenant law governs deposits, repair, entry, rent and ending a tenancy, often in ways a lease cannot change. The property management agreement sets an agent's authority, fees, reporting and exit. A hotel management agreement needs budget approval, a workable performance test and clear exit terms. Draft all three for the place you build.

Next: Sage on The Numbers: a lease-up schedule and a hotel fee worked step by step.
checklist: My lease form was drafted for the jurisdiction by a local lawyer.
I know the local rules on deposits, entry notice, rent increases and ending a tenancy.
The property manager's leasing rent range and spending limit are written limits.
Rents and deposits are held in a trust or client account in my name.
The management agreement requires a monthly rent roll, bank reconciliation, arrears report and funnel.
Any hotel management agreement gives me budget approval and a performance test I have tested with numbers.
I know how either side may end each agreement and how records are handed over.
I have budgeted for arrears and the legal process of recovering possession.
head: Field checklist
speak: A rental building runs on three sets of rules. Landlord-tenant law, which in many places protects tenants in ways a lease cannot waive: limits on deposits, duties of repair, notice before entry, rules on rent increases and a defined legal process to end a tenancy, with self-help eviction prohibited in many places. The property management agreement, which makes the manager my agent with written limits on leasing and spending, a fee, monthly reporting, money held in trust and a clear exit. And for a hotel, the management agreement, where I need budget approval, a performance test I have tested with real numbers, limits on central charges and terms for a sale. In Canada tenancy is mostly provincial with tribunals; in Guyana it descends from common law with rent restriction legislation whose scope must be confirmed locally. In both, I start from the statute and the forum, never a borrowed lease form.
terms: Habitability — the legal standard that rented homes be fit to live in, which many regimes impose regardless of the lease.
Self-help eviction — removing a tenant without a court or tribunal process, for example by changing locks, prohibited in many places.
Performance test — a clause in a hotel management agreement allowing the owner to terminate if results fall below an agreed benchmark for a set period.

hostile.q: As the operator, we will not accept any performance test. Our brand needs long-term certainty. Why should we?
hostile.a: Because certainty has to run both ways. I am committing the building to your brand for many years and giving you control of operations. In return I need a way out if the hotel consistently underperforms its competitive set and its budget, with a cure right for you. We can discuss the benchmark, the period and the cure, but an agreement with no performance test asks me to carry all of your risk, and my lender will ask the same question.

title: A Lease-Up Schedule and a Hotel Fee, Worked Step by Step
summary: Two calculations sit under every rental and hotel opening: a month-by-month lease-up schedule that finds the operating deficit and the break-even month, and a hotel management fee calculation that shows who carries the risk when results fall. This lesson works both forward with hypothetical round numbers and units.
body:
A lease-up schedule tells you the month your building stops costing you money, and a hotel fee calculation tells you who carries the risk when the market softens. Both take a page of arithmetic, and both should be done before you open.

Recall

Q. What is a performance test in a hotel management agreement?

A. A clause allowing the owner to terminate if the hotel's results fall below an agreed benchmark, such as RevPAR against a competitive set and profit against budget, for a set period, usually with a cure right for the operator.

Q. What is effective rent?

A. The rent actually earned after concessions, spread over the lease term; one free month on a 12-month lease at 2,200 dollars face rent gives about 2,017 dollars.

Q. What is RevPAR?

A. Revenue per available room: room revenue divided by rooms available, or average daily rate multiplied by occupancy.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an odd week, so we work forward. On Day 3 you estimated the operating deficit from an average. Today you build it month by month, which is how a lender will want to see it and how you will manage it. Then you price a hotel management agreement's fees across a good year and a weak one, so you can see the operating leverage an owner carries. Every figure is hypothetical and round.

Part one: the lease-up schedule

In plain English: start with the units let on opening day, add the net leases each month, work out the average units paying rent in each month, multiply by rent, subtract costs, and keep a running total.

The inputs. 120 units. Stabilised occupancy 95 percent, which is 114 units. Pre-leased before opening: 24 units. Net absorption after opening: 12 units a month. Effective rent: 2,017 dollars a unit a month. Monthly costs: operating costs 90,000 dollars plus interest of about 128,300 dollars on a 22,000,000-dollar loan at 7 percent, total about 218,300 dollars.

Step 1, occupancy at the end of each month: 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96, 108, then 114 in month 8, capped at stabilisation.

Step 2, average occupied units in each month, the midpoint of the start and end: 30, 42, 54, 66, 78, 90, 102 and 111.

Step 3, revenue, average units times 2,017 dollars.

MonthAverage unitsRevenueCostsSurplus or deficit
13060,510218,300minus 157,790
24284,714218,300minus 133,586
354108,918218,300minus 109,382
466133,122218,300minus 85,178
578157,326218,300minus 60,974
690181,530218,300minus 36,770
7102205,734218,300minus 12,566
8111223,887218,300plus 5,587

All figures are in dollars per month. Step 4, the cumulative deficit across months 1 to 7 is about 596,200 dollars, and month 8 is the first in surplus. Step 5, the break-even occupancy: costs of 218,300 dollars divided by 2,017 dollars is about 108 units, or 90 percent.

Say that out loud now.

Two lessons sit inside the table. First, pre-leasing is worth real money. On Day 3, with no pre-leasing and a 10-month lease-up, the deficit was about 1,030,000 dollars; here 24 pre-leased units and a faster pace bring it to about 596,000. Second, the break-even sits high, at 90 percent, because interest is more than half the monthly cost. A building with high leverage reaches break-even late, so leverage makes lease-up more expensive as well as riskier. Run the same table at 8 units a month and stabilisation slips to month 12 and the deficit rises by about half, to roughly 890,000 dollars; that is the slow case your reserve should cover.

Part two: a hotel management fee across two years

A second worked example. A 150-room hotel. The management agreement pays the operator a base fee of 3 percent of total revenue and an incentive fee of 8 percent of gross operating profit, known as GOP, the profit after operating departments and undistributed operating expenses, before fees, fixed charges and debt. These fee levels are commercial practice for the illustration, not a standard.

Good year. Average daily rate 180 dollars, occupancy 70 percent, so RevPAR is 126 dollars. Room revenue is 150 rooms times 365 nights times 126 dollars, about 6,898,500 dollars. If rooms are 75 percent of total revenue, total revenue is about 9,198,000 dollars. GOP at a 35 percent margin is about 3,219,300 dollars. Base fee: 3 percent of 9,198,000, about 275,900 dollars. Incentive fee: 8 percent of 3,219,300, about 257,500 dollars. Total fees about 533,400 dollars.

Weak year. Occupancy falls to 60 percent, so RevPAR is 108 dollars, room revenue about 5,913,000 dollars and total revenue about 7,884,000 dollars. Costs do not fall as fast as revenue, so the GOP margin falls to 30 percent, about 2,365,200 dollars. Base fee about 236,500 dollars; incentive fee about 189,200 dollars; total about 425,700 dollars.

Now compare. Revenue fell about 14 percent. GOP fell about 27 percent. The base fee fell only 14 percent, because it is tied to revenue, not profit. Profit after both fees fell from about 2,685,900 dollars to about 1,939,500 dollars, a fall of about 28 percent, borne almost entirely by the owner. That is operating leverage, and it is why owners push for a larger share of the operator's pay to sit in the incentive fee and, often, for the incentive fee to apply only after the owner has received a priority return.

Part three: reading the schedule as a lender does

A lender reading your schedule asks three questions, and you should answer them on the same page. First, is the absorption assumption evidenced? Show the leasing pace of comparable new buildings and your own pre-leasing. Second, what happens on the slow case? Show the table at 8 leases a month beside the base case, with the month each reserve runs out. Third, when will the take-out sizing test be met? If the take-out lender requires three months of stabilised effective rent, the test is met not in month 8, when you first reach 114 units, but in month 10 or 11, after the trailing period has passed. Interest and operating costs keep running in those months, but so does income, so the cost is small; the timing, however, is what your construction loan maturity has to allow for. If the construction loan matures in month 9, you have a maturity gap, and that is the conversation to have with the lender before you open, not at maturity.

Write the three answers on the schedule itself. A schedule with its own stress case and its own timing test is one a credit officer can approve quickly. A schedule that shows only the base case invites the lender to build its own slow case, and its version will be more conservative than yours.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing the deficit reserve on the base case and discovering the slow case in month 4. The control is a monthly lease-up schedule at two absorption rates, with the reserve sized on the slower one and the break-even occupancy stated.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares hotel operators by their headline fee percentage. Compare them by total fees and owner's profit in a weak year, because that is when the structure of the fee matters.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught break-evens and downside cases. The lease-up break-even here, 90 percent occupancy, is that idea in its most practical form: the line the leasing team must cross each month before the building stops consuming your cash.

Recap

Build lease-up month by month: here, 24 pre-leased units and 12 leases a month gave a deficit of about 596,000 dollars, break-even at 90 percent and surplus from month 8. A hotel with a revenue-based fee passed most of a weak year's 27 percent fall in GOP to the owner.

Next: Remi in The Room: the meeting with the property manager when lease-up is running slow.
checklist: I build the lease-up schedule month by month, not from an average.
I count pre-leased units at opening and show their value in the deficit.
I know my break-even occupancy and how leverage moves it.
I run the schedule at two absorption rates and size the reserve on the slower one.
For a hotel, I calculate fees and owner's profit in a good year and a weak year.
I compare operators on total fees and owner's profit in the weak year, not the headline percentage.
I know whether the incentive fee applies before or after any owner's priority return.
head: Field checklist
speak: I build lease-up month by month. In my hypothetical 120-unit building, 24 units are pre-leased and 12 more lease each month, at 2,017 dollars effective rent, against about 218,300 dollars a month of operating costs and interest. Averaging the occupied units in each month and subtracting costs gives deficits that shrink from about 158,000 dollars in month 1 to about 12,600 in month 7, a cumulative deficit of about 596,000 dollars, with surplus from month 8. Break-even is about 108 units, 90 percent, because interest is more than half the cost. At 8 leases a month the deficit rises to roughly 890,000 dollars, so I size the reserve on that. For a hotel, a base fee on revenue and an incentive fee on gross operating profit mean that when occupancy falls from 70 to 60 percent, profit after fees falls about 28 percent and the owner carries most of it.
terms: Break-even occupancy — the occupancy at which collected revenue just covers operating costs and debt service.
Gross operating profit (GOP) — a hotel's profit after operating departments and undistributed operating expenses, before management fees, fixed charges and debt service.
Operating leverage — the effect of fixed costs making profit fall faster than revenue when revenue declines.

hostile.q: As the lender, your break-even is 90 percent occupancy. Isn't that too thin a margin above stabilised occupancy of 95?
hostile.a: It is thin, and I agree it is the key risk. That is why the deficit reserve is sized on a slow case of 8 leases a month, why 24 units are pre-leased before opening and why I am not drawing the take-out until occupancy has held at 95 percent on effective rent for the period you define. If you want more headroom, I would rather reduce the take-out amount slightly than lengthen the lease-up assumptions.

title: The Meeting With the Property Manager When Lease-Up Runs Slow
summary: Four months after opening, occupancy is well behind plan and the property manager arrives with a fix: deeper concessions, looser tenant screening and fewer maintenance staff. This lesson runs the meeting: diagnose the leasing funnel before changing the price, protect the rent roll a lender will read, and keep the decisions in writing. It closes with a monthly note on working with advisers.
body:
When lease-up runs slow, the first instinct in the room is to cut the price. The better first move is to find out where in the funnel the tenants are being lost, because a price cut fixes only one of the four places a lease-up can stall, and it is the one that costs you value permanently.

Recall

Q. In yesterday's schedule, what was the break-even occupancy, and why was it so high?

A. About 108 units, or 90 percent, because interest on the construction loan was more than half the monthly cost.

Q. What does a property manager's agreement need to say about authority?

A. It should set written limits, such as the rent range at which the manager may sign leases and the spending limit for repairs without the owner's approval.

Q. What is the question behind the question?

A. The real concern or aim under what someone actually asks, which you answer if you want to settle the matter rather than only the words.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in the room: the regional manager of your third-party property management firm, the on-site leasing manager and your asset manager, who watches the numbers for you. You chair. The building opened four months ago. The plan had it 72 percent leased; it is 58 percent leased. Every month of delay costs you roughly 100,000 dollars of operating deficit on the hypothetical numbers from this week, and the take-out lender will size on the effective rent of the leases signed now. The manager has three proposals. Each one would raise occupancy faster, and each one carries a cost you will pay for years.

Hold your state. A slow lease-up feels urgent, and urgency is when people agree to things they later regret. Decide before you walk in that you will leave with a diagnosis and a plan, not only a price change.

First, the funnel

Before any proposal, ask for the leasing funnel for the last eight weeks: enquiries, tours, applications, approvals and move-ins. Say: "Before we talk about price, show me where we are losing people."

A worked example, hypothetical. Enquiries are on plan at 120 a month. Tours are 70, on plan. Applications are 18, against a plan of 30. Approvals are 15 of the 18. So the building is attracting interest and visits, but people who see it are not applying. That is not mainly a price problem at the enquiry stage; it is something the visitors see or hear. Ask: "What are people saying at the end of the tour?" The leasing manager answers: the gym is unfinished, the corridor carpets are still covered, and the parking allocation is unclear. Those are fixable in weeks, and none of them needs a permanent price cut.

Say that out loud now.

Proposal one: two free months

The regional manager: "The building across the road is offering two months free. We need to match it."

The question behind the question: is the manager, who is paid on collected revenue and judged on occupancy, choosing the fastest route to its own target?

Say: "I understand. Two free months on a 12-month lease cuts effective rent by about 17 percent, and the take-out lender will read it in every lease we sign now. Let us fix what the funnel shows first. If applications are still below plan in four weeks, I will consider a targeted concession on the slowest unit types, recorded in the rent roll."

Never say: "Do whatever it takes to fill it." That sentence is an unlimited authority, and the manager will use it.

Proposal two: looser screening

The leasing manager: "We are declining applicants with weaker credit. If we approve more, we fill faster."

The question behind the question: will today's occupancy be bought with tomorrow's arrears?

Say: "Our screening criteria stay as written, and they must comply with the law on discrimination. If you think a criterion is stricter than our market needs, bring me the data and we will change it formally, for everyone." A tenant who cannot pay costs months of lost rent and a legal process to recover the unit, which LEX covered on Day 4. An arrears problem in year one is a lower NOI at take-out.

Proposal three: fewer maintenance staff

The regional manager: "To cut the deficit, we can reduce the maintenance team from three to two until we stabilise."

Say: "No. The first maintenance call is the moment a new tenant decides whether to renew. We are spending to win tenants; we should not save money on the thing that keeps them." Then stay silent and let the asset manager speak to the numbers. A third technician costs a small fraction of one month of deficit.

What the asset manager adds

Turn to your asset manager last, and ask for one thing: "Show us the take-out position if we do nothing different, and if we add the targeted concession." The asset manager answers with two numbers, the effective rent and the implied take-out loan under each plan. That turns the conversation from occupancy, which is the manager's measure, to value, which is yours. It also shows the regional manager, without any argument, why you are being careful. People accept a constraint more readily when they can see the number behind it, and the number came from your own side of the table rather than from your mood.

Closing the meeting

Read back the decisions: the gym and corridors finished within three weeks, the parking allocation published, a tour script reviewed by the asset manager, no change to screening, maintenance staffing unchanged, and a review of the funnel in four weeks with a pre-agreed concession on the two slowest unit types if applications have not reached plan. Ask the manager to confirm the rent roll will show face rent, concessions and effective rent for every lease. Send the minutes the same day.

Working with advisers, a monthly thread

A property manager is an adviser and an agent at once, and its interests overlap with yours without being the same. Its fee depends on collected revenue, its reputation on occupancy, and it does not carry your loan or your take-out gap. That is not a reason to distrust it. It is a reason to know where its incentives point before you take its advice, which is the same discipline Week 25 taught for lawyers, accountants and engineers.

A practical habit is to ask every adviser one question before you act on a recommendation: "What would you advise if you were paid the same whatever I decided?" The answer is usually close to the original. When it is not, you have learned something about the recommendation, and the adviser usually respects you more for asking.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in this room is a permanent concession agreed to solve a temporary problem. The control is a rule that every concession is diagnosed against the funnel, limited to defined unit types and periods, recorded in the rent roll and reviewed against the take-out lender's sizing test.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads occupancy as the measure of success. The lender and the buyer read effective rent, arrears and renewals. Ask for all four.

Callback

In Week 123, Marco's site meeting asked for the record that would decide each problem before deciding it. This is the same meeting in a different phase. The funnel is the leasing equivalent of the test register: the evidence that tells you which fix the problem actually needs.

Recap

Diagnose the funnel before you change the price. Fix what visitors see first, keep screening and maintenance as they are, and use concessions only where the funnel shows a price problem, recorded and limited. Know where every adviser's incentive points before you take its advice.

Next: Kema on the week in review: lease-up, the rent roll and the Red Pen.
checklist: I ask for the eight-week leasing funnel before discussing any price change.
I know where the funnel is losing people: enquiries, tours, applications, approvals or move-ins.
Every concession is limited to defined unit types and periods and recorded in the rent roll.
I check each concession against the take-out lender's sizing test before approving it.
Tenant screening criteria change only formally, for everyone, and within the law.
Maintenance staffing is protected during lease-up.
Before acting on advice, I ask what the adviser would recommend if paid the same whatever I chose.
head: Field checklist
speak: When lease-up runs slow, I do not start with the price. I ask the property manager for the leasing funnel: enquiries, tours, applications, approvals and move-ins. In my hypothetical, enquiries and tours were on plan but applications were 18 against 30, so visitors were seeing something that put them off: an unfinished gym, covered carpets, unclear parking. Those I fix in weeks. The manager wanted two free months, which cuts effective rent by about 17 percent and shows in every lease the take-out lender reads, so I agreed only a targeted, recorded concession if applications are still short in four weeks. I kept the screening criteria and the maintenance team, because arrears and poor service cost more than they save. I closed with written actions and dates, and I remembered that a manager paid on revenue and judged on occupancy will naturally reach for the fastest fix.
terms: Leasing funnel — the stages from enquiry to tour, application, approval and move-in, measured to show where prospective tenants are lost.
Arrears — rent that is due and unpaid.
Asset manager — the owner's representative who oversees the property manager and the building's financial performance against the business plan.

hostile.q: As your property manager, I am telling you the market moved. If you will not match two free months, you will be at 60 percent for another quarter. Who carries that?
hostile.a: I do, and I have priced it: about 100,000 dollars a month of deficit, which is reserved. Two free months would cost me about 17 percent of effective rent on every lease signed now, and the take-out lender sizes on those leases for years. Your own funnel says visitors are touring and not applying, so let us fix what they see first. If applications have not reached plan in four weeks, we will use a recorded concession on the two slowest unit types, and I will review it with you then.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 125 Review: Lease-Up, the Rent Roll and the Red Pen
summary: This review tests the week on lease-up: the curve, effective rent, the operating deficit, the take-out, landlord-tenant law, management agreements and the slow-lease-up meeting. The Red Pen drill then finds the planted defects in a hypothetical rent roll summary, and the boardroom drill asks you to explain lease-up in two minutes.
body:
Lease-up comes down to one discipline: report the income a lender or buyer can rely on, which is effective rent from lawful leases, collected in cash, and manage the months before it as a funded deficit rather than a surprise.

Recall

Q. In the slow lease-up meeting, what did the funnel show, and what did you fix first?

A. Enquiries and tours were on plan but applications were well below, so visitors were put off by what they saw; the unfinished gym, covered carpets and unclear parking were fixed before any price change.

Q. What is Rule 124?

A. Never let a buyer's deposit fund anything but the building it was paid for; hold deposits in protected trust or escrow, sell only what the funded plan can finish and never use pre-sale cash for land or another project.

Q. From Week 117, what does retainage protect against?

A. It holds back part of each payment until completion as a cushion against defects, incomplete work and, where it is a statutory holdback, unpaid subcontractors.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Kema. Lease-up is where three years of development become one number that a take-out lender and every future buyer will test: stabilised net operating income. This review rehearses the explanations you will need when someone asks why your rent roll is worth what you say, and the Red Pen shows how quickly a rent roll can mislead its own author.

The six questions

Question 1. What decides a lease-up?

Answer: Four things: the pace, set by absorption; the real rent, which is effective rent after concessions; operations, which decide renewals; and the rent roll, which a lender or buyer tests lease by lease. Plan all four during construction.

Question 2. What is effective rent on a 2,200-dollar lease with one month free over 12 months?

Answer: 11 months times 2,200, which is 24,200 dollars, divided by 12, about 2,017 dollars a month, about 8.3 percent below face.

Question 3. How did a permanent concession reach the take-out loan?

Answer: It lowered stabilised NOI from about 1,929,600 to about 1,678,800 dollars. At an 8 percent debt yield the take-out fell from about 24,120,000 to about 20,985,000 dollars, below the 22,000,000-dollar construction loan, creating an equity call of about 1,015,000 dollars.

Question 4. What is Rule 125?

Answer: Never underwrite or borrow against a rent you have not tested, lease by lease, against the law that governs that lease, and treat any rent that depends on a change in a tenant's legal status as a legal risk to be priced. It comes from Stuyvesant Town.

Question 5. What do you need in a hotel management agreement as owner?

Answer: Budget and capital plan approval, a performance test I have tested with real numbers, limits on central charges, clear terms on key money and on a sale, and an exit. All of it is negotiated commercial practice.

Question 6. Why does high leverage make lease-up more expensive?

Answer: Because interest is a fixed monthly cost, so break-even occupancy rises. In the worked schedule, interest was more than half the cost and break-even was 90 percent, so the building consumed cash until late in lease-up.

Say that out loud now.

Recap

Remi framed lease-up as turning a building into a business. Ford, with Cole, took Stuyvesant Town through seven steps: a price and a loan sized on deregulations a court later held were not permitted. Sage priced the operating deficit and the take-out. LEX set out tenancy law and management agreements, with Canada and Guyana compared. Sage built a lease-up schedule and a hotel fee. Remi ran the slow lease-up meeting from the funnel, not the price.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical rent roll summary, prepared for a take-out lender, and find the defects before reading on.

Rent roll summary, month 9. Units: 120. Occupied: 112, 93 percent. Average rent: 2,200 dollars. Annualised rent: 2,956,800 dollars. Concessions: standard. Arrears: minimal. Deposits: two months' rent held in operating account. Units 401 to 410 let to a related company at market rent. Stabilised: yes.

The defects. One: average rent is face rent; with one free month on recent leases, effective rent is about 2,017 dollars, so annualised rent is overstated by about 246,000 dollars. Two: "concessions: standard" hides the number a lender sizes on; show concessions lease by lease. Three: "arrears: minimal" is a feeling, not a figure; state the amount and the ageing. Four: deposits held in the operating account, rather than a trust or separate account, may breach the lease, the management agreement or the law, and two months may exceed a local cap; confirm with counsel. Five: ten units let to a related company are not arm's-length leases, and many lenders exclude or discount them, which may take occupancy below the stabilisation test. Six: "stabilised: yes" depends on the lender's definition, usually a sustained period at a stated occupancy, which one month cannot prove. Fixed, the summary is less flattering and far more useful.

The boardroom drill

Explain lease-up to a board in two minutes. Set a timer and speak before you read the model.

Model answer: "Lease-up turns our finished building into a business. We are paying the full operating cost and interest from opening, so until occupancy passes about 90 percent we run an operating deficit, which we have reserved on a slow case. The take-out loan that repays construction is sized on stabilised NOI using effective rent, after concessions, from the most recent leases. So every concession we offer now reaches the take-out and the value; a permanent free month would cut value by several million dollars. We diagnose slow leasing through the funnel before we change price. Every lease is on a locally drafted form, and every rent we underwrite is lawful, which is Rule 125, from Stuyvesant Town. And our managers work under written authority limits, report monthly and hold money in trust."

What a weak answer sounds like

Compare the model with a weak version: "We are 93 percent leased, rents are strong and we expect to refinance soon." Each phrase invites a question. Leased on what definition, and how many of those leases are to related parties? Strong rents measured at face or effective, and against which comparables? Refinance when, on what sizing test, and what is the gap to the construction loan if the test is met? The weak answer is not dishonest; it simply offers a feeling where the board needs a figure with a source.

When you record yourself, listen for the words strong, soon, minimal and standard. In the Red Pen summary, two of them were standing exactly where a number belonged. Replace each with the figure and its source, and record again. The second version will be shorter, more confident and much harder to argue with, because it contains nothing the listener has to take on trust.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a rent roll written to reassure rather than to be tested. The control is a summary that states effective rent, concessions, arrears and related-party leases as figures, reconciled to signed leases and bank receipts.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner declares stabilisation the first month occupancy reaches target. A lender wants it held. Report the trend, not the peak.

Callback

In Week 123, the construction checkpoint ended with the chain of verification: nothing done, paid or accepted until someone independent proves it. Lease-up extends the same chain into operations. A rent is not income until it is lawful, collected and reconciled.

Recap

Lease-up is pace, effective rent, operations and the rent roll. Fund the deficit on a slow case, size the take-out on effective rent, test every rent against the law, write management agreements with authority limits, reporting and exits, and report figures, not feelings.

head: The six questions
speak: Lease-up turns a finished building into a business, and four things decide it: pace, effective rent, operations and the rent roll. From opening day I pay full operating costs and interest, so I run a deficit until occupancy passes break-even, about 90 percent in my hypothetical, and I reserve for it on a slow case. The take-out loan is sized on stabilised NOI using effective rent from recent leases, so a permanent free month cut my hypothetical take-out from about 24.1 to about 21 million dollars and created an equity call. Rule 125, from Stuyvesant Town: I test every rent against the law that governs its lease before I underwrite or borrow against it. My leases are drafted locally, my managers work under written limits, and my hotel agreement has budget approval and a performance test. When I Red Pen a rent roll, I look for face rent posing as income, vague arrears, deposits in the wrong account and related-party leases.
terms: Annualised rent — the current monthly rent roll multiplied by twelve, which overstates income if face rent is used where concessions apply.
Related-party lease — a lease to a person or company connected to the owner, which lenders often exclude or discount when testing occupancy and income.
Arrears ageing — a breakdown of unpaid rent by how long it has been overdue, such as under 30, 30 to 60 and over 60 days.

hostile.q: As the take-out lender's credit officer, ten of your occupied units are let to a company you control. Why should I count them?
hostile.a: You should not count them as arm's-length leases, and I have shown them separately. Without them, occupancy is 102 of 120, 85 percent, below your stabilisation test, so I am not asking you to fund yet. The related company will either be replaced by third-party tenants over the next two months or the leases will be terminated, and I will report occupancy and effective rent on your definitions until the test is met for the full period.
